parameters.name: result_column
parameters.description: The column from which the matching value is retrieved and returned.
parameters.examNote: This is the column in the lookup table that holds the value you want to bring back — equivalent to the return column in a VLOOKUP.

parameters.name: search_column1
parameters.description: The column to search in. Must be in the same table as result_column.
parameters.examNote: Multiple search column/value pairs can be provided to create a composite key lookup. All conditions must match simultaneously — they are AND-ed together.

parameters.name: search_value1
parameters.description: The value to match in search_column1. Typically a column reference from the table being calculated.
parameters.examNote: If search_value1 comes from a different table, the tables do not need a defined relationship. This is the key advantage of LOOKUPVALUE over RELATED.

parameters.name: alternate_result
parameters.description: The value returned when no match is found. Defaults to BLANK() if not specified.
parameters.examNote: Unlike the last argument in some functions, LOOKUPVALUE's alternate_result is positional — it must come after all search_column/search_value pairs.

returnType: Scalar (value from result_column where search conditions match), or alternate_result if no match
summary: LOOKUPVALUE retrieves a value from a column in another table based on one or more matching criteria, without requiring a defined relationship between the tables. It is DAX's equivalent of a VLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH. Use it when you need to bring values from an unrelated table, or when a relationship cannot be created due to data quality issues or model design constraints. If multiple rows match all conditions, an error is returned — use IFERROR or ensure uniqueness.

examples.label: Retrieve manager name without a relationship
examples.explanation: For each row in Sales, LOOKUPVALUE searches Employees[EmployeeID] for the value in Sales[SalesRepID]. When E101 matches, it returns the corresponding Employees[ManagerName] value 'Sarah Jones'.

examples.label: Composite key lookup
examples.expression: Price = LOOKUPVALUE(PriceList[Price], PriceList[ProductID], Sales[ProductID], PriceList[Year], Sales[Year])
examples.explanation: Both ProductID AND Year must match simultaneously. This is equivalent to a two-column VLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH with multiple criteria. Both conditions are AND-ed together.

steps: Scan search_column in search_table for search_value
When a match is found, return the corresponding value from result_column
If no match found: return BLANK (or alternate_result if specified)
If multiple matches: error — use relationship or SELECTEDVALUE instead

commonTraps: If multiple rows in the lookup table match all search conditions, LOOKUPVALUE returns an error — not BLANK. Use IFERROR(LOOKUPVALUE(...), BLANK()) or ensure uniqueness before relying on LOOKUPVALUE.
LOOKUPVALUE works without a defined relationship. If a relationship already exists between the tables, use RELATED instead — it is simpler, faster, and leverages the model's relationship engine.

LOOKUPVALUE returning BLANK on no match can silently hide data issues in an RLS scenario. Always validate that all expected values have matches, especially when used for security-sensitive calculations.

sqlEquivalent.expression: SELECT e.ManagerName FROM Sales s LEFT JOIN Employees e ON s.SalesRepID = e.EmployeeID
sqlEquivalent.note: SQL uses a JOIN to retrieve values from another table. LOOKUPVALUE achieves a per-row lookup without a physical join or a defined model relationship. For performance at scale, defined relationships with RELATED are preferred over LOOKUPVALUE.
